title: Red Hat RHCSA
summary: The Red Hat Certified System Administrator, usually called the RHCSA, is Red Hat's entry level certification for Linux administrators and carries the exam code EX200. It is aimed at engineers who already touch Red Hat Enterprise Linux in their daily work and want proof that they can configure, secure and repair a real server. Every task is performed on live systems, so an employer reads a pass as evidence of practical ability rather than memorized theory. The objectives are grouped into the ten areas listed below, and Red Hat publishes no percentage weight for them, so treat each area as equally important. The structure follows the published objectives; check the vendor's current version before booking. Passing RHCSA is also the usual first step towards the Red Hat Certified Engineer credential and towards roles such as Linux administrator or site reliability engineer. This page is an independent study guide and is not affiliated with Red Hat.

beginner.definition: The RHCSA is a certification from Red Hat for people who look after Linux servers. The letters stand for Red Hat Certified System Administrator, and the exam code is EX200. You do not answer only multiple choice questions. The whole exam is a set of practical tasks on a live system. Red Hat does not publish a percentage weight for each objective area.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many employers treat the RHCSA as the first real proof that you can work on Linux servers. It shows that you can manage users, storage, services and security without step by step instructions. Because the exam is practical, a pass shows that you can repair a broken system while the clock runs. The certification also opens the door to more advanced Red Hat credentials, such as the Red Hat Certified Engineer. For an early career engineer, that combination often leads to a junior Linux administrator or site reliability role.
howItWorks: Build a practice machine first. Install Red Hat Enterprise Linux or AlmaLinux in a virtual machine. Then you can break it and rebuild it without fear.
Work through the published objectives in order. Read one task, close your notes, then perform the same task again from memory.
Practice on the command line every day. Typical jobs include creating users, extending logical volumes, fixing permissions and opening firewall ports.
Reboot the practice machine after each session. Many tasks must still be correct after a restart, so a reboot is the simplest check.
Learn to read the built in documentation. During the exam you may use manual pages and command help, so practice finding answers there.
Run timed laboratory sessions. Give yourself a fresh machine and a list of tasks, then work without looking anything up.
beginner.example: Picture a small company where you are the only person who looks after the servers. On Monday your manager asks for three things. You must add a new disk, create a shared folder for one team, and allow web traffic. You do all three in a terminal and then reboot the server. On Tuesday you check the machine again. The disk is still mounted. The shared folder still belongs to the right group. The firewall rule still allows web traffic. That is exactly the kind of work the RHCSA exam measures. The tasks are small, but the examiner checks the final state of the machine, not the commands you typed.
takeaways: The RHCSA is a practical exam, so time on a real system matters far more than reading.
Red Hat publishes no percentage weights, so every objective area deserves attention.
Always check the current objectives on the Red Hat website before you book.

objectives: Explain what the RHCSA certification proves to a hiring manager
Describe how a performance based Linux exam is marked
Build a study routine around a personal practice machine
Name the ten objective areas covered by the exam
Recognize which tasks must survive a system reboot

chapters.title: Understand and use essential tools
objectives: Run commands at a shell prompt with correct syntax, including pipes and redirection
Search text with grep and basic regular expressions
Create, copy, move and delete files and directories, including hard and soft links
Read and change standard user, group and other permissions
Archive and compress files with tar, gzip and bzip2
Connect to remote systems with SSH (Secure Shell)
Find answers in manual pages, info pages and files under /usr/share/doc

chapters.title: Create simple shell scripts
objectives: Write a script that makes a decision with if and test
Repeat work with for and while loops
Read arguments such as the first and second positional parameter
Capture the output of a shell command inside a script
Check the exit code of a command and act on the result

chapters.title: Operate running systems
objectives: Boot, reboot and shut down a system in a controlled way
Switch the system into a different systemd target by hand
Interrupt the boot process to recover access to a system
Find processes that use the most processor or memory and stop them
Adjust process scheduling priority with nice and renice
Apply a tuning profile to the running system
Read and preserve system log files and the journal
Start, stop and check the status of a network service

chapters.title: Configure local storage
objectives: List, create and delete partitions on MBR (Master Boot Record) and GPT (GUID Partition Table) disks
Create and remove physical volumes, then assign them to volume groups
Create and delete logical volumes
Mount a file system at boot by UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) or by label
Add a partition, a logical volume or swap space to a system without destroying existing data

chapters.title: Create and configure file systems
objectives: Create, mount, unmount and use vfat, ext4 and xfs file systems
Mount and unmount a network file system with NFS (Network File System)
Extend an existing logical volume and grow the file system on it
Create a set group ID directory so that a team can share files
Configure disk compression and layered storage
Diagnose and correct file permission problems

chapters.title: Deploy, configure and maintain systems
objectives: Schedule tasks with at and cron
Install and update software packages from a remote repository or a local source
Work with package module streams
Configure a service to start automatically at boot
Set the default boot target and modify the system bootloader
Configure a time service client so that the system clock stays correct

chapters.title: Manage basic networking
objectives: Configure IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) and IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) addresses
Configure hostname resolution so that names resolve to addresses
Configure network services to start automatically at boot
Restrict network access with firewall-cmd and firewalld

chapters.title: Manage users and groups
objectives: Create, change and delete local user accounts
Set passwords and adjust password aging for local accounts
Create, change and delete local groups and group memberships
Configure superuser access for a chosen user or group

chapters.title: Manage security
objectives: Configure firewall settings with firewall-cmd and firewalld
Create and use file access control lists
Configure key based authentication for SSH
Set enforcing and permissive modes for SELinux (Security Enhanced Linux)
List and identify SELinux file and process contexts
Restore default file contexts and change SELinux boolean settings
Diagnose and address routine SELinux policy violations

chapters.title: Manage containers
objectives: Find and retrieve container images from a remote registry
Inspect a container image
Run, start, stop, list and remove containers with podman and skopeo
Run a service inside a container
Configure a container to start automatically as a systemd service
Attach persistent storage to a container
